name: Core LLD Behavioral Patterns: State, Strategy & Observer in Practice
tagline: Eliminating brittle if-else chains in LLD by encapsulating lifecycle transitions (State), interchangeable algorithms (Strategy), and event notifications (Observer).
purpose: Learn when and how to combine State, Strategy, and Observer cleanly without creating shared-state race conditions or listener memory leaks.

spark.summary: Behavioral patterns—State, Strategy, and Observer—eliminate brittle if-else chains in Low-Level Design interviews and production systems by encapsulating lifecycle transitions, interchangeable algorithms, and event notifications behind clean interfaces.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use State when behavior changes with an object's internal lifecycle (Vending Machine, Order), Strategy when algorithms vary independently (Pricing, Dispatch), and Observer when decoupled listeners react to state changes.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Although State and Strategy share nearly identical UML class diagrams, their **intent** is distinct: **State**: Context delegates to a `State` object representing its current lifecycle phase; transitions happen *inside* states as actions occur.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Vending Machine State Transitions (IDLE -> HAS MONEY -> DISPENSING); Parking Lot Exit: Strategy Fee + State Release + Observer Board (ExitGate -> PricingStrategy -> SpotState -> DisplayObserver).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Balance class proliferation against extensibility. Two production pitfalls trip up teams using behavioral patterns: storing instance-specific fields inside shared singleton `State` objects (causing cross-request race conditions).

**Failure Modes & Application:** See State, Strategy, and Observer applied end-to-end in classic object-oriented system design problems.

learningJourney.title: What are State, Strategy, and Observer
learningJourney.explanation:
Although State and Strategy share nearly identical UML class diagrams, their **intent** is distinct:
- **State**: Context delegates to a `State` object representing its current lifecycle phase; transitions happen *inside* states as actions occur.
- **Strategy**: Context delegates an algorithm (e.g., pricing, routing) to an injected `Strategy` interface that can be swapped without changing lifecycle.
- **Observer**: A Subject maintains a thread-safe listener set and pushes domain events to decoupled subscribers.

learningJourney.title: Why hardcoded switch/if-else chains fail the Open/Closed Principle
learningJourney.explanation:
In both LLD interviews and production codebases, requirements evolve: 'add weekend flat-rate pricing', 'add a Maintenance state', or 'notify an audit webhook on dispense'.

When all transitions and algorithms live in one giant `switch(status)` block, every new feature modifies tested core logic and risks breaking unrelated branches. Behavioral patterns isolate each new state, algorithm, or listener into its own cohesive class.

learningJourney.title: Clean Java interfaces for State, Strategy & Observer
learningJourney.explanation: Keep `State` implementations stateless (no per-machine mutable fields if shared as singletons) and store listeners in `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for safe concurrent iteration.
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Pattern Classes vs. Enum State Machines vs. Event Bus

benefits: Full polymorphism and Open/Closed extensibility per state.
Compact, singleton-safe, zero extra files for fixed small state sets.
costs: Harder to inject external Spring/DI dependencies into enum constants.

comparison.choice: Async Event Bus vs. Sync Observer
benefits: Async bus prevents slow observers from blocking the core transaction.
costs: Introduces eventual consistency and ordering considerations.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Avoiding Singleton State Corruption & Observer Leaks
learningJourney.explanation: Two production pitfalls trip up teams using behavioral patterns: storing instance-specific fields inside shared singleton `State` objects (causing cross-request race conditions), and registering short-lived UI/request observers without `unsubscribe()` (leaking memory).

ideas.title: Stateless Transitions
ideas.description: Pass the Context (`ParkingSpot`, `VendingMachine`) into every `State` method and mutate fields only on the Context.

ideas.title: Weak/Explicit Unsubscribe
ideas.description: Always pair `subscribe()` with deterministic `unsubscribe()` or `AutoCloseable` handles.
